extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and scholars in communication and cultural studies
extracted.subtask_description: Articulating a cultural/ritual framework for studying communication as a symbolic process that produces, maintains, repairs, and transforms reality; contrasts this with the transmission/information view and proposes related research questions and ethical concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of communication as a symbolic process
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication is a symbolic process whereby reality is produced, maintained, repaired, and transformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central analytic move: treat communication not merely as transmission of information but as the activity that brings realities into being, sustains them, fixes breakdowns, and enables transformation. Use this fourfold functional frame (produce/maintain/repair/transform) when defining or analyzing communicative phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two distinguishing properties of symbolic forms: displacement and productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Each symbolic form (visual maps, oral songs, kinesthetic dances, language) allows displacement — representing things not present — and productivity — generating an infinity of representations from a finite set of elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or describing a symbolic medium, note how it enables reference to absent objects/events (displacement) and how a finite grammar or set of elements can produce novel utterances or mappings (productivity). Examples in the text: maps (lines/names), poems/songs (mnemonic streams), ritual dances (movement mappings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols have a dual capacity: 'of' and 'for' reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic artifacts can function both as representations 'of' reality (descriptive, indexical) and as representations 'for' reality (templates that produce or guide the realization of that reality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the blueprint example: a blueprint can describe a house (symbol 'of') and also serve as the plan to build it (symbol 'for'). Recognize this duality in evaluating texts, media, rituals — they may both describe a social state and actively produce dispositions/behaviors consistent with that description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought as predominantly public and social
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is argued to be largely public and social — it occurs on blackboards, in dances, in recited poems — depending on a public stock of symbols; private thought is derivative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyses of cognition, rhetoric, or pedagogy, foreground materially available symbolic systems and shared external representations (maps, plays, diagrams) rather than treating thought as exclusively private mental activity. Evaluate how public symbols enable 'running' models faster than real-world trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of communication are both representations 'of' and templates 'for' communication (reflexivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication models do not only describe processes; they also shape and produce the communicative behavior and institutions they purport to explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat theoretical models as interventions with ethical and social effects: e.g., transmission models generate policies privileging power/control, ritual models emphasize community. When constructing or applying models, assess how they might reconfigure practice and institutional arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast of transmission view and ritual view
rubrics_metrics.description: Transmission view: communication as information transfer, instrumental, linked with power, administration, economics, and individualistic/conceptual language. Ritual view: communication as shared symbolic action sustaining community, aesthetic and fiducial functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media, pedagogy, or policy, explicitly locate the analysis within or between these paradigms. Note that each implies different research questions, ethical implications, and historical/technological associations; be wary of uncritical dominance of the transmission frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key research questions for communication studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions the discipline must answer include: How are significant symbolic forms created, apprehended, and used? What differences exist between forms (art, science, journalism, religion, common sense, mythology)? What are historical and comparative variations? How do communication technologies influence what can be created and apprehended? How do groups struggle over the definition of reality?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these explicit questions as an agenda-setting rubric for empirical and theoretical work: formulate projects that address creation/use of symbolic systems, comparative/historical change, technological effects, and conflicts over reality construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical reflexivity: models carry ethical implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Models of communication have ethical implications because, in their 'for' aspect, they produce different forms of social relations and thus instantiate normative consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that analyses and interventions in communication explicitly consider ethical consequences: whose interests do models serve, what social relations do they instantiate, and how might they be altered to promote restorative communal values rather than merely political/economic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate communication technologies and institutions by their social uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether new communication technologies and institutional arrangements are devoted to expanding people's powers to learn and exchange ideas and experience, or primarily harnessed for politics, economics, and therapy (which can narrow cultural purposes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging technologies, education systems, or urban design, examine dominant uses and incentives: e.g., has education been turned into citizenship/professionalism/consumerism/therapy? Are cities designed primarily for automobiles and trade? Use this as a normative criterion for recommending restorative, community-oriented redesigns of communicative models and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps/representations shape perceived reality (selection and simplification matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representations (maps, models, poems, dances) simplify and select features of environments; different mappings produce different realities — living under different maps is living in different realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation of media texts, pedagogical materials, or policy frames, analyze what is left out by a representation, whose perspective it foregrounds, and how that selection configures possible behaviors and experiences. Treat representational choices as constitutive, not merely descriptive.
